presentingComplaint: Sudden severe chest tightness, pounding palpitations and acute breathlessness for the past 2 hours.
history: A 52-year-old man was brought to the emergency department after abruptly developing crushing central chest tightness, a thunderous frontal headache and drenching sweats while sitting at his desk. Within 30 minutes he became severely breathless and could not lie flat. He describes similar but milder self-limiting episodes over the preceding 4 months - sudden spells of palpitations, pallor, pounding headache and anxiety lasting 15-30 minutes, often triggered by bending or straining, each time attributed to ‘panic attacks’. He has lost roughly 6 kg over 3 months despite no dieting. He was noted at a recent pharmacy check to have a blood pressure of 190/110 and was started on amlodipine, with little effect. No prior cardiac history, no exertional symptoms between spells, non-smoker. The paramedic ECG and troponin prompted an initial working diagnosis of acute coronary syndrome, but the ED consultant was struck by the strikingly labile blood pressure - oscillating between 230/130 and 90/60 within minutes without intervention - and the episodic prior history.
examination: Anxious, diaphoretic and pale, sitting bolt upright. Cool peripheries with tremor. Marked beat-to-beat blood-pressure lability documented on the arterial line, swinging from severe hypertension to transient hypotension. Bibasal fine crepitations to mid-zones with a gallop rhythm consistent with acute pulmonary oedema. No focal neurological deficit, no goitre, no lid lag. Abdomen soft, no bruit or palpable mass.
imaging: Portable CXR: bilateral perihilar alveolar oedema with upper-lobe diversion, normal cardiac silhouette. Bedside echo: hyperdynamic then transiently hypokinetic LV with apical ballooning pattern (stress cardiomyopathy), no significant valve lesion. CT abdomen (once stabilised): 4.5 cm heterogeneous right adrenal mass with avid, patchy enhancement and central necrosis.
microbiology: Not applicable - non-infective presentation. Blood cultures not indicated.
differentialDiagnoses: Acute coronary syndrome (troponin-positive chest pain with ECG changes)
Hypertensive emergency with flash pulmonary oedema
Thyroid storm (adrenergic surge with tremor, tachycardia, weight loss)
finalDiagnosis: Phaeochromocytoma crisis - catecholamine-induced cardiomyopathy with flash pulmonary oedema and troponin elevation, mimicking acute coronary syndrome; confirmed by grossly elevated plasma/urinary metanephrines and a 4.5 cm enhancing right adrenal mass.
citations: Endocrine Society - Pheochromocytoma and Paraganglioma Clinical Practice Guideline - 2014
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e - Pheochromocytoma
stewardship: Not applicable - non-infective endocrine emergency; no antibiotics indicated.
contraindications: Do NOT give beta-blocker before adequate alpha-blockade - unopposed alpha stimulation precipitates hypertensive crisis and worsens pulmonary oedema
Avoid drugs that provoke catecholamine release (metoclopramide, glucagon, unopposed beta-agonists)
Avoid biopsy of the adrenal mass - risk of precipitating fatal crisis
edgeCases: Blood pressure may be paradoxically normal or hypotensive between paroxysms, masking the diagnosis
Catecholamine cardiomyopathy can be reversible with alpha-blockade and tumour resection despite troponin rise
Coronary angiography often shows unobstructed coronaries despite an ACS-like presentation
expectedMaiK: Recognise a phaeochromocytoma crisis behind an ACS/hypertensive-emergency mimic: markedly LABILE blood pressure plus a prior history of paroxysmal headache-palpitations-sweating spells is the key. Confirm biochemically with plasma free (or 24h urinary fractionated) metanephrines, then localise with CT/MRI adrenals. Control the crisis with alpha-blockade FIRST (e.g. phentolamine / phenoxybenzamine), add a beta-blocker only after alpha-blockade, and refer for surgical resection after adequate preoperative alpha-blockade.
expectedNextQuestions: Are there prior episodic spells of headache, palpitations, pallor and sweating (paroxysmal pattern)?
Is the blood pressure labile/fluctuating rather than fixed?
Any family history of phaeochromocytoma, MEN2, VHL, NF1 or paraganglioma?
Any recent unexplained weight loss, tremor or heat intolerance to weigh against thyroid storm?
expectedInvestigations: CT / MRI of the adrenal glands and abdomen
TSH and free T4 to exclude thyroid storm
